young.html: Claude Lévi-Strauss (say LAY-vee STROWSS) was a French anthropologist, a scientist who studies human cultures. As a young man he traveled deep into Brazil to live with peoples there. Later he read thousands of myths from North and South America and asked: is there a hidden pattern in how people tell stories?

He thought there was. People everywhere, he said, think in pairs of opposites: day and night, hot and cold, raw and cooked, land and sky, life and death. Stories often take two opposites and find something in between that joins them, like a bridge.

young.name: gb-ls-pairs
young.cap: Tap each pair of opposites, then find the "in-between" that some myths use to join them (our simple examples).

young.html: Opposites in stories. Think of a favorite fairy tale. Find two opposites in it (rich and poor, forest and castle, young and old). Is there a character or place that is in between, and joins them? Draw the two ends and the bridge.

full.html: Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) taught in São Paulo in the 1930s and made expeditions among peoples of the Brazilian interior, which he later described in Tristes Tropiques (1955). During the Second World War he escaped occupied France to New York, where he met the linguist Roman Jakobson. From Jakobson he took the idea that would shape his life's work: that the methods of the new science of language could be used on all of culture. Structural Anthropology (1958) collects his essays on that method.
No excerpts here. The book was first published in English in 1963 and is under copyright. This lesson describes it in our own words. Library copies are easy to find.

Structural linguistics showed that the sounds of a language mean nothing by themselves; what matters is the system of contrasts between them. In English, "pat" and "bat" are different words only because p and b contrast. Speakers use this system without being aware of it. Lévi-Strauss proposed that kinship rules, myths and customs are also systems of contrasts, working below awareness, and that the anthropologist's job is to find their structure.

His first example is family relations. He looked at four relationships: husband and wife, brother and sister, father and son, and a mother's brother and her son. In many societies, he found, these relations come in balanced pairs: where a boy's relation with his father is strict, his relation with his mother's brother is easy, and the reverse. He called this small system the atom of kinship.

Myths seem to say anything at all, yet similar myths appear across the world. Lévi-Strauss proposed breaking a myth into its smallest units of meaning, which he called mythemes, and arranging them by their relations rather than their order in the story, like the parts of an orchestra score. On this view a myth works on a contradiction a society cannot resolve, such as that between life and death, by finding a chain of mediators that softens it.

full.name: gb-ls-mediation
full.cap: His example from North American myths: how a hard opposition is softened step by step (our drawing of his scheme).

full.html: In his example, life and death are bridged by farming (which gives life) and war (which brings death); between those stands hunting, which takes life to sustain it. Then among animals, plant-eaters and beasts of prey are bridged by carrion-eaters such as the raven and the coyote, which eat meat but do not kill. That, he suggested, is why raven and coyote so often appear as the trickster, a go-between, in these myths.

Structuralism was one of the most influential movements in mid-20th-century thought, spreading from anthropology to literary criticism, psychology and philosophy. Lévi-Strauss became a public figure in France and lived to be a hundred. Critics have raised several objections. His structures are hard to test: a clever analyst may find opposites anywhere. His method tends to set aside history, change and the choices of individual people. Anthropologists such as Clifford Geertz preferred to interpret cultures through the meanings people themselves give them, while materialist anthropologists such as Marvin Harris argued that customs are best explained by ecology and economy. Later thinkers, the "post-structuralists," questioned whether stable structures exist at all. His studies of kinship and myth are still read as classics, and the search for patterns he began goes on in many forms.
Thinking Lévi-Strauss said all cultures are the same. He held that all human minds work with the same kind of logic, and that this produces endless different systems.

items: Frazer's Golden Bough, an earlier rung, compared customs as evidence of stages of thought; Lévi-Strauss compared them as structures with their own logic.
Sophocles' Oedipus, in the Greek rungs, is the myth he analyzed most famously, laying its episodes out in columns.
Rousseau, whom Lévi-Strauss called, in a 1962 lecture, the founder of the sciences of man.
Wittgenstein said meaning lies in use; Lévi-Strauss looked for meaning in hidden contrasts. Compare the two.
Do all people think in pairs of opposites?
Can a pattern exist in a culture if nobody in it knows the pattern is there?
Why do similar stories turn up in places far apart?
How could you tell whether a pattern is really in the myths or only in the mind of the analyst?

questions: What pairs of opposites can you find in a story you know well?
Why do tricksters, like a clever fox or coyote, appear in so many stories?
Can you follow rules you could not explain, like the grammar of your own language? Give an example.
Lévi-Strauss's critics said a clever person can find patterns anywhere. How would you test a pattern?
What would you want to learn if you could live for a year with a people very different from your own?
